entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

You shuffle to the door in your hobbles, put your face to the gap, and call it out in Goblin, flat as a hanged man: Greyshaft's books are honest, honest as the knife at your sister's throat. The Foreman smiles faintly at the sound. Then you turn, swing your chained fists down, and the lantern goes off the desk. It hits the flagstones and bursts, and burning oil runs across the desk, the floor and the tails of the ledgers. The Foreman, quick as a cat, hops clear of it with his hem untouched.

That is the last thing that goes your way. The flames light the room, and the cloaks stop pretending. The blade at Tessa's neck comes across and she goes down in a heap, her hand still closed on the hairpin, and her wrist-lock lies open beside her. A bolt from the shutters takes you in the ribs, and you fold. Another is levelled at your back, and the Foreman lifts one soft hand and says, "Not that one. I want him breathing." The bolt stays in the bow.

You lie on hot stone. You're unconscious, at 0 hit points, and the smoke is rising. Tessa is down a pace away, and her chest is moving. In your darkness there is one thing you can feel, and it is a drumbeat. It is the Tallies' spears on the stair, and it is much closer than it was. A door is splintering. You have one death save passed, and two more to go.

It is your turn, but you can't act. You are unconscious and bleeding. A little after ten in the morning, the ledger-house is on fire.

sheet.name: Korvash Emberhide
sheet.opening: Korvash Emberhide, a hulking red-scaled dragonborn barbarian (Chaotic Good, loud, proud, quick to anger; ideal Charity; bond: he keeps his word no matter what; flaw: inflexible), arrives at dusk in a lowland market town near the foot of the mountains, driving off a pack of bullies shaking down a family of herders, as he has done for years. His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. Hook for the opening: just after the bullies flee, a frightened young herder or a traveler brings him word, perhaps carried from Aunt Veshra, that a hobgoblin warband bearing a tin-masked captain and a notched rod has been seen again, or that something connected to the Goat's Throat has turned up. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. entries.text: notebook: updated Gorrak Vael

You shuffle to the door in your hobbles like a beaten man and call it through the gap in flat Goblin: Greyshaft's books are honest, honest as the knife at your sister's throat. On the last word you bring your chained fists down across the lantern. It shatters, and burning oil runs over the desk and up the Foreman's sleeve.

He stands too close and has no time to step back. The flame climbs his arm, he claws at the sleeve, and his small voice, for once, is not tidy. The fire takes more of him than he can bear. He goes down beside the desk and doesn't get up.

The room breaks in two. The cloak who held the blade at Tessa's neck lowers it and backs away, staring at the man on the floor. Two more drop their points. Three do not. They have no paymaster, but they have swords and a prisoner in front of them. Tessa strains at her wall-ring and the pick slips. Then the pommel comes down on you again, and you hear the oak splinter as you fall.

My ruling: with the Foreman dead and the door breaking, the three who fought on struck to knock you down and did not finish you.

You wake on a bench in the ledger-house in the white light of early afternoon, with a cloth under your head and the iron gone from your wrists. It is about one o'clock, and you have 1 hit point.

The room is full of Tallies. The door hangs off one hinge. Three grey cloaks lie dead along the wall, and three more kneel under Dreg's spear. The burned shape of the Foreman has been covered with a cloak. Tessa sits beside you with her wrist rubbed raw and a cup of water in her hands. She tips it to your mouth, and her eyes are bright.

Gorrak Vael stands at the barred bedchamber door with his face bare, his ribs bound, and his arms folded. He hasn't touched the bar. "The book is behind this door," he says quietly, in Common. "I would not open it until you woke, Emberhide. It is your fire. I want to see how you spend it." Dreg stands at the doorway with his spear grounded and doesn't look at either of you. Out on the walk, the Tin Row's leavings are being brought up from the deep shaft into the light.

You drop behind a boulder, out of the archers' line, and shout your terms down the slope. Call off the bowmen, meet at the ford-stones, blades and shields only. If you win, Brakk and his nine lay down their arms and walk to Harrowmere. If he wins, your spears go home and the barrel is his.

The silence runs long. Then Brakk laughs once, short and dry. "Done," he calls. "On the ford-stones, then. Bows unstrung, you have my word." He raises a hand, and on the roof both archers lower their bows and make a show of slackening the strings. The three shield-men at the foot of the track step aside.

You whistle two notes back toward the gully. Within a few minutes Ushk comes up the goat-path at a crouching run, helm in hand, with Hale labouring behind him. The six Tally spears stay hidden in the gully, as you said. Ushk looks down at the yard and his face tightens. "He gave his word on the bows," he murmurs, "and I have never known his word to be worth the breath. Look at the wall by the stones." You look. Two hunched shapes lie in the tumbled stonework beside the ford-stones, where the dark water runs. They have not moved, and they have not been called off.

Hale grunts. "Two in the wall, and he's counting on you not seeing them. Archers' strings are slack for show; I can see one thumb still on a nock." He spits. "Man's honest the way a fox is honest."

Below, Brakk walks out of the yard alone, shield on his arm and longsword drawn, the ring glinting in his ear. He stops on the flat ford-stones and waits, easy, back to the stream. Behind him the fold-house wall holds nine silent watchers.

It's a quarter past seven. You have your rage and your breath weapon ready, Ushk and Hale beside you, and a path down to the ford. What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 27 ~7:05 AM: Korvash challenged him to single combat at the ford-stones. Brakk refused the terms: he will keep his archers, and says he'll meet Korvash at the stones only with his shield-line beside him. He has sent a man to the barrel and wants the matter settled before Ushk's spears can close. Stalling for time.

entries.text: notebook: updated Brakk
time: 4 minutes later: Day 27, 7:07:06 AM

You drop behind a boulder, out of the archers' line, and shout your terms down the slope. Call off the bowmen, meet you at the ford-stones with blade and shield, no ambush. If you fall, he and his nine lay down their arms and walk to Harrowmere. If he wins, your spears go home and the barrel is his. Then you whistle two notes back toward the gully, and you feel your breath and your rage waiting in your chest like coals under ash.

The answer takes a while. Brakk's laugh is short and humourless. "A fine speech, Emberhide. You have your father's mouth." He doesn't move from the rock. "No. The archers stay. I've buried too many men who trusted a clean fight. If you want the stones, come down and stand on them, and my shield-line will stand beside me. Or don't."

It isn't a refusal of the fight. It's a refusal of your terms. Behind him you see a lean hobgoblin slip along the tumbled wall toward the ford-stones, where the barrel lies, and begin prying at a flat slab. Brakk is not hurrying. He is buying time.

Boots scrape on scree behind you. Ushk comes up the goat-path at a crouch, helm on, with Hale a pace behind him breathing hard and the six Tally spears strung out below. Ushk looks down at the yard and his face goes grey. "That's him," he says softly. "That's the stance. He's already counted us, Emberhide."

The two archers on the roof haven't lowered their bows. The path below is a single file of loose stone with the shield-line waiting at its foot, and the ford-stones are open ground beyond. Hale mutters that there's a second way down on the east side, a sheep-drop through broken rock, steep enough to break a pony's leg but not a man's. It's a few minutes past seven. Brakk's man is working at the slab.

Two arrows hiss over the boulder and crack against rock behind you, and a splinter of stone cuts your cheek. Brakk himself stays where he is, back to the rock, watching with his sword down. Behind you, Ushk's boots are coming up the scree at a run, with Hale and six spears a short way behind. The shield-men have perhaps twenty paces of path left before they reach you.

Your rage and your breath are both ready, and you hold the high ground. Roll for initiative when you've told me what you do first.
